[remote server](remote-servers.md) it lists that computer's files; a server
running an older Muxy asks to be updated first.

## Links and files

- `Cmd`-click a URL or file path to open it. Paths with `:line:column` jump to
  that line in supporting extensions.
- Enabled extensions register supported file types. One match opens directly;
  multiple matches show a searchable chooser. Turn on **Always use for this
  type** before choosing to save a default.
- **Settings → General → Files** manages custom patterns, per-type defaults,
  rule priority, and when the chooser appears. Unmatched local files and folders
  go to Finder or the system file manager.
- The project-app picker in the topbar only opens the project when clicked;
  it never controls terminal file links.
- Web links open in your system browser, or in the
  [built-in browser](browser.md) when **Settings → Browser** says so.
- Dropping files on a terminal pastes their paths.
- On a [remote server](remote-servers.md), dropped and pasted files are
  uploaded first and the remote path is pasted. `Cmd`-clicking a remote file
  opens a matching extension, or offers remote-file actions including a read-only copy.

## Shell integration

With [shell integration](server.md#shell-integration), Muxy tracks each
terminal's folder, and you can:

- Jump between prompts with `Cmd+Up` and `Cmd+Down`.
- Select a command's output with **Select Command Output** in the Edit menu or
  the right-click menu.

## Program status

Tabs show the progress a program reports with OSC 9;4 or the
[program status protocol](https://www.superlogical.com/rex/docs/build/program-status)
(OSC 7501), which wins when a program sends both. Working and waiting clear
when the program exits; a reported error stays until the next report. Scripts
can report with `muxy status`, for example
`muxy status working --app deploy --msg "Uploading"`.

## Quick Terminal

A terminal that drops down from the top of the screen from anywhere. Record a
global shortcut in **Settings → Quick Terminal** first; none is set by default.

It keeps one terminal in Home, hides when it loses focus, and has its own size
and transparency settings. Click the pin button to keep it open and above other
windows on every desktop; Muxy remembers the choice. `Cmd+W` closes it and ends
its terminal, whatever the close setting, unless another pane still shows it.

## Appearance and configuration

Fonts, colors, transparency, vibrancy, cursor, padding, selection, scrolling,
and key bindings are in **Settings → Terminal**, saved to `terminal.toml`.
Themes are in **Settings → Appearance**. See
[Settings](../user-guide/settings.md#terminal-configuration).

- `Cmd+=` and `Cmd+-` change the focused pane's font size. `Cmd+0` resets it.
- `Option` acts as `Alt` by default (configurable in Terminal settings).
- Programs can show images with the Kitty graphics protocol, Sixel, or iTerm2
  inline images. Kitty images can also be passed as a file, a temporary file,
  or shared memory, by programs on the computer that runs the terminal. Muxy
  reads only regular files. As in Kitty and Ghostty, it deletes a temporary
  file or shared memory once it has read the image. Kitty's PNG format also
  accepts JPEG, GIF, WebP, BMP, TIFF and ICO files. Pictures over about a
  million pixels are scaled down to fit. Raw pixels sent with the Kitty
  protocol show at full size up to about two million pixels, and larger ones
  are scaled down to that. Programs that replace their image many times a
  second, such as `mpv --vo=kitty` or remote desktop viewers, play smoothly:
  each picture stays until the next is ready.
- Animated images play in the desktop app: animations a program sends with
  the Kitty graphics protocol, and animated GIFs shown as iTerm2 inline images
  or through Kitty's PNG format. A GIF sent through Kitty's PNG format plays
  when the same command sends and shows it; one sent first and placed later
  shows its first frame. GIFs play without end. A GIF whose frames pass about
  32 MB is scaled down to fit, and a very long one loses its last frames. A
  terminal keeps about 136 MB of images; past that, the oldest ones go, as in
  Kitty and Ghostty. A saved screen keeps the frame that was showing.
- Images stay with their rows when output pushes them into scrollback, and
  scrolling back shows them again, as stills. A terminal's saved history,
  read after it ends or the server restarts, keeps only its text.

# Layout Examples

Save any of these in a project's `.muxy/layouts/` folder.

## `side-by-side.yaml`

```yaml
layout: horizontal
panes:
  - tab:
      name: editor
      command: nvim .
  - tab:
      name: shell
```

```
┌──────────────────┬──────────────────┐
│ editor           │ shell            │
│ nvim .           │                  │
└──────────────────┴──────────────────┘
```

## `stacked.yaml`

```yaml
layout: vertical
panes:
  - tab: npm run dev
  - tab:
      name: shell
```

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
│ npm run dev                         │
├─────────────────────────────────────┤
│ shell                               │
└─────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## `quad.yaml`

```yaml
layout: horizontal
panes:
  - layout: vertical
    panes:
      - tab: { name: top-left }
      - tab: { name: bottom-left }
  - layout: vertical
    panes:
      - tab: { name: top-right }
      - tab: { name: bottom-right }
```

```
┌──────────────────┬──────────────────┐
│ top-left         │ top-right        │
├──────────────────┼──────────────────┤
│ bottom-left      │ bottom-right     │
└──────────────────┴──────────────────┘
```

## `dev.yaml`

```yaml
layout: horizontal
panes:
  - tab:
      name: editor
      command: nvim .
  - layout: vertical
    panes:
      - tab:
          name: server
          command:
            - npm install
            - npm run dev
      - tab:
          name: shell
```

```
┌──────────────────┬──────────────────┐
│ editor           │ server           │
│ nvim .           ├──────────────────┤
│                  │ shell            │
└──────────────────┴──────────────────┘
```

# Layouts Overview A layout is a file in your project that describes a tab of split terminals. Check it in, and anyone on the project can open the same workspace with one click. ```mermaid flowchart LR FILES[".muxy/layouts/*.yaml"] --> PICK["Apply Layout…"] PICK --> CONFIRM{"Confirm"} CONFIRM -->|"yes"| TABS["Project tabs replaced
commands run"] ``` ## Pages | Page | What's in it | | --- | --- | | [Schema](schema.md) | Fields, splits, and the JSON form | | [Examples](examples.md) | Ready-to-copy layouts | ## How it works - Put layout files in `.muxy/layouts/` inside a project or worktree folder. Remote projects work too. - Use `.yaml`, `.yml`, or `.json`. The file name, without its extension, is the layout's name. - Apply one from the project's menu with **Apply Layout…**, or from the layout button in the tab bar. The button appears when the project has at least one layout. - Layouts are never applied automatically. - Applying asks first, then replaces all of the project's tabs in this app, pinned tabs included, and runs the layout's commands. Terminals that no app shows anymore end. - Layouts are a desktop app feature. The `muxy` terminal UI does not read them. Only apply layouts you trust: their commands run as you. ``` my-project/ .muxy/ layouts/ dev.yaml release.yaml ```

# Layout Schema

A layout is a tree. Each leaf is one terminal (`tab`). Each branch splits its
`panes` side by side or stacked. The whole tree opens as one tab, titled after
its first terminal.

## A single terminal

```yaml
tab:
  name: editor
  command: nvim .
```

A bare string is a command:

```yaml
tab: htop
```

## Splits

```yaml
layout: horizontal
panes:
  - tab:
      name: editor
      command: nvim .
  - layout: vertical
    panes:
      - tab: npm run dev
      - tab:
          name: shell
```

Splits can nest up to 32 levels. Panes in a split share its space evenly.

## Fields

| Field | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `layout` | `horizontal` (side by side) or `vertical` (stacked). Defaults to `horizontal`. |
| `panes` | A non-empty list of child nodes. Makes the node a split. |
| `tab` | The terminal of a leaf: a command string, or an object with `name` and `command`. |
| `tab.name` | Optional title. Defaults to the command's first word, or `Terminal`. |
| `tab.command` | Optional command, or a list of commands joined with `&&`. Runs in the project folder. |

```yaml
tab:
  name: setup
  command:
    - npm install
    - npm run dev
```

## Legacy `tabs`

Older layouts with a `tabs` list still load. The first entry fills the leaf;
the others open as separate tabs. Use `tab` in new layouts.

```yaml
tabs:
  - name: editor
    command: nvim .
  - name: shell
```

## JSON

The same schema works in `.json` files:

```json
{
  "layout": "horizontal",
  "panes": [
    { "tab": { "name": "editor", "command": "nvim ." } },
    { "tab": "npm run dev" }
  ]
}
```

## Limits

A layout file can be up to 256 KiB, nest up to 32 levels, and hold up to 64
terminals.

# App model How people use Muxy: the apps, navigation, settings, and updates. ## The apps | App | Connects to | | --- | --- | | Desktop app (macOS) | The server on the same computer, starting it if needed, and the servers of other computers over SSH or after pairing with them. | | `muxy` terminal UI | The server on the same computer, starting it if needed, or with `--host`, the server on another computer over SSH. Ships with the desktop app and also on its own. | | Phone app | A paired computer's server, over the local network or a VPN, or any computer's server over SSH. | Every project knows which server it lives on. The desktop app works with every server at once: the sidebar lists each server under its own heading, **This Mac** (**This Computer** on Linux) first, then the other computers' servers in the order of the Servers popover. A heading shows how its server is doing and expands or collapses its Home and projects. This computer's starts expanded and the others collapsed; each app remembers the choice in `settings.toml`. Opening something in a collapsed server expands it, and expanding a server whose projects aren't known yet connects to it. Other computers' servers start disconnected each time the app opens, until you connect one or open one of its projects or tabs. **Show other servers in the sidebar** in Settings → Appearance hides the other servers' headings and projects, leaving this computer's. Remote projects are marked with their server and path where they show outside the sidebar. Terminals another client shows on this computer's server, such as another desktop, the terminal UI, or a phone, open here too, as tabs in their project that don't take focus. Terminals nobody shows, such as detached ones or ones made with `muxy session create`, and those other clients show on another computer's server stay in **Existing Terminals**. Closing or detaching such a tab here leaves the terminal running in the clients still showing it, and the app doesn't open it here again. The **Servers** section at the bottom of the sidebar shows each remote server's state. Its popover adds servers (host, user, port, key file, or a password that Muxy asks for and keeps only in memory) and manages them. **Pair with Link…** adds another computer from the link its **Settings → Servers** shows instead, with no SSH setup. A paired computer can't be restarted from here, and pairing again from its **Edit…** form recovers one that was revoked or reset. When a server lacks Muxy, a released app offers to install the same version there; when its version can't talk to the app, the section explains how to update it. Removing a server only forgets its projects in this app. **Manage Servers…** opens **Settings → Servers**, where everything about servers and their clients lives: - This computer's server: **Connect** while it is offline, or **Restart Server…** and **Stop Server…**, then the [server settings](../features/server.md#settings) for its sessions. - **Clients** lets phones and other computers connect to this computer's server: **Allow clients** turns access on. While it is on, **Pair a client** shows a pairing code and link, and **Push notifications** pauses or resumes notifications to paired phones, asking first when phones would stop getting them. **Clients** lists the paired ones to revoke, or to reset a phone's notifications. A code that wasn't copied is withdrawn once the page leaves the screen; a copied link stays valid until it is used or expires. `muxy mobile` does the same without the desktop app. - **Other Servers** lists every remote server by group, and connects, disconnects, regroups, or removes several at once. Disconnecting leaves a server's terminals running there. **Add Project** (the row below each server's projects, or the sidebar's filter menu in **Focus Current Project**) offers **Folder…** on that server and its **Recently Removed** projects. ⌘O does the same on the current project's server. ⌘O searches folders that aren't projects yet and completes typed paths with Tab; **Finder…** (**Browse…** on Linux) picks one in the system dialog instead. Enter adds the folder as a project with a terminal, or opens a terminal in the project it already is. Missing folders require an explicit creation confirmation. **New Tab in Project…** (⌘⇧N) lists every server's saved projects, each marked with its server, and the other computers' servers, then matching folders on the current project's server, or on this computer while that server isn't connected. Enter opens a terminal in the project, or at a folder in its computer's Home; ⌘Enter adds the folder as a project with a terminal. On another computer's server it browses that server's folders, connecting first if needed. A server in the list browses its folders, or with ⌘Enter opens a terminal in its Home. A server's menu in the Servers popover offers **New Tab** and **Add Project…** too. Files and images dropped or pasted on a remote terminal, or sent from the composer, are copied to that computer and its path is pasted. Clicking a file path in a remote terminal offers a read-only copy here, or its path. Each app keeps its own layout: tabs, splits, workspaces, and project order. Projects and terminals are shared, and a computer's terminals open as tabs in its own desktop app. Several `muxy` windows can open the same terminal UI layout. ## Navigation ```mermaid flowchart LR FILTER["Workspace filter"] --> SIDEBAR["Project sidebar"] SIDEBAR --> PROJECT["Project"] --> TAB["Tab"] --> PANE["Focused pane"] ``` - The sidebar shows **All projects** by default. Pick a workspace to filter it. Home stays first and worktrees appear under their parent. - One project order applies under every filter. - Picking a project shows its tabs. - A window has one focused pane. Closing it moves focus to a neighbor. Closing a tab moves focus to the next tab, or the previous one. Closing something in the background never steals focus. ## Moving tabs and panes Tabs and panes move anywhere on the same computer. Terminals keep running and pages keep their state. A terminal moved to another project belongs to it on the server too, so removing the old project no longer ends it. Servers too old to do that refuse the move. - Drag a tab from the tab bar or the tab sidebar onto another place in the tabs, onto a project, or out of the app into a window of its own. - Drag a pane by its header, or with Command held, into another tab's splits, onto the tab bar or a sidebar row as a new tab, onto a project, or out of the app into a window of its own. - While dragging, a chip follows the pointer, the drop place is outlined or marked between tabs, and a place on another computer shows as refused. - A tab in its own window has the system's window controls and leaves the main window's tabs. Drag its titlebar over the main window to put it back, or use **Move to Main Window**. Closing the window closes the tab. Tab windows reopen where they were after a restart. - The pane header of a tab window is its titlebar: it holds the window's controls and moves the window. A tab window shows a titlebar of its own only when no pane header runs along its top. - The tab menu offers **Move to New Window** and **Move to Project**; the pane menu adds **Move to New Tab** and, in a tab window, **Move to Main Window**. The command palette has **Move Tab to New Window**, **Move Pane to New Tab**, and **Move Pane to New Window** for the main window. - A terminal still starting can't change project until it has started. - A terminal can also float over the main window instead, over its own project or over every project. A floating terminal is a tab outside the tab bar, like a tab window drawn inside the main window, and its panes move the same ways. See [Floating terminals](../features/terminal.md#floating-terminals). On Linux, panes and tabs move between windows through these menus, and a drag out of the main window opens a window of its own. Only macOS follows a drag from one window into another, since Linux doesn't tell apps where their windows are on screen. ## Opening and restoring - The desktop app restores all projects, tabs, and window state on launch. It never opens a tab by itself, except for terminals another client shows on this computer's server, which open as tabs. Until the [welcome tour](#welcome-tour) is finished or skipped, it opens over them. - When a terminal's session is gone because the server stopped, as after restarting the computer, its pane keeps its place and starts a new shell in the folder it was last in. The program that ran there doesn't start again. - The terminal UI opens one shell in Home the first time, then restores its layout. - `muxy `, or on macOS dropping a folder on the Dock icon or using **Open With**, opens the folder in the desktop app. It selects the folder's project on this computer or adds one, then opens a new terminal tab there. Without the desktop app, or over SSH, `muxy ` opens in the terminal UI. - **Existing Terminals** lists a project's terminals that this app isn't showing, and which app owns each one. Opening one adds it to your layout. On this computer's server, the ones other clients show open as tabs by themselves, so it lists the detached ones and those closed here. ## Welcome tour On launch, a short tour opens until it has been finished or skipped, on new and existing installs alike. Its nine steps cover how the server and apps fit together, projects, extensions, AI agents, the composer, remote servers, the phone app, and shortcuts. - **Skip Tour** or Escape ends it on any step. Clicking outside does not, and quitting partway shows it again from the start on the next launch. - It sets things up only when asked. **Add a Project…** and **Add a Server…** open the usual dialogs, and the tour returns when they close. **Install & Enable** installs and enables the ticked extensions, Files and Git by default, after listing what each one asks for. They finish even if the tour closes first. - **Pair a Phone** turns on **Allow clients** if it is off and shows a pairing code in the tour. Leaving the step withdraws the code, and turns access back off if the tour turned it on and nothing paired. - Dragging the dimmed area, the art, or the tour's top bar moves the window. - **Welcome Tour** at the top of Settings, or **Show Welcome Tour** in the command palette, replays it. Each profile remembers this as `onboarding_completed` under `[appearance]` in `settings.toml`. ## Worktrees New Worktree has a name, a new or existing branch, and Default, Template, or Folder location choices. Worktrees default to `~/.muxy/worktrees//`. Settings → General sets the global location; each project remembers its choice. Templates support `{branch}`, `{base-dir}`, and `{project-name}`. Optional setup and teardown commands come from the source project's `.muxy/worktree.json` and `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/muxy/worktree.json` (by default, `~/.config/muxy/worktree.json`): ```json { "setup": ["npm ci"], "teardown": ["docker compose down"] } ``` Review and enable commands when creating or removing a worktree; `muxy worktree` runs them only with `--hooks`. Setup runs per-machine commands first; teardown runs project commands first. Commands run in the worktree, with `MUXY_PROJECT_PATH` and `MUXY_WORKTREE_ID`, `MUXY_WORKTREE_PATH`, `MUXY_WORKTREE_NAME`, and `MUXY_WORKTREE_BRANCH` available. A setup failure keeps the new worktree; a teardown failure stops removal. ## When things go away | Situation | What you see | | --- | --- | | The server is offline | Projects stay visible, terminals keep their last screen, and web panes keep working. Edits and closes are replayed on reconnect. | | A remote server drops | Its section shows it offline and it reconnects on its own, waiting longer each time, until a login or host key needs you. Its projects never show as failed while offline. | | A project's folder is gone | The project shows as failed, also on a remote server. | | A terminal ends | Its panes close in every app, including hidden tabs. | | The server stops, or the computer restarts | Tabs and splits stay, each showing its last screen. Once the server is back, every terminal pane starts a new shell in the folder it was last in. | | You quit or detach | Terminals keep running. On macOS, only while Muxy is on under Background App Activity; otherwise macOS ends them and the next launch shows how to turn it on. | | **End All Sessions and Quit** | Every terminal on this computer ends and its panes close. Other panes stay. | The status bar shows the current project's server. Its popover connects, restarts, or stops it. ## Proxy The status bar's **Proxy** popover sets up one HTTP or SOCKS5 proxy, with an optional login, kept privately and left out of backups. **Use for the whole app** sends new terminals on this computer, Muxy's own downloads, and SSH to remote servers through it. Otherwise, right-click a terminal and choose **Apply Proxy**: it restarts in the same folder with the proxy, and its tab shows a proxy icon. Terminals get the proxy as `http_proxy`, `https_proxy`, `all_proxy`, and `no_proxy`. Running terminals keep what they started with. ## Settings - Settings opens in a single tab, on this computer. Opening it again selects the existing tab. It works while offline, and changes apply immediately. - App preferences live in `settings.toml`, terminal preferences in `terminal.toml`, and custom themes in `themes/`. `muxy config` reads and changes both files and the running app applies the change, and **Ask Agent…** at the top of Settings starts a coding agent that changes them for you. - Every app shortcut can be changed in Settings → Keyboard. Terminal key bindings are set in Settings → Terminal, and the Quick Terminal shortcut has its own setting. Normal keystrokes in a terminal always go to the terminal. - **Settings → Terminal → Selection → Word selection characters** controls which extra characters stay with letters and numbers when double-clicking or dragging by words in the desktop app. The default `/.-_~:@?&=%+#` keeps common paths and URLs together. Whitespace always separates words. To restore selection of only letters and numbers, clear the field. In `terminal.toml`, this is `selection_word_chars` under `[options]`. - **Settings → Appearance → App language** picks the interface language. English is built in; other languages come from language-pack extensions, the same ones made for Muxy 1.x. Untranslated text stays English, and while the chosen pack is unavailable Muxy shows English. - Server settings, such as the shell and history size, apply to this computer's server. `muxy --host` changes another computer's. Stopping or restarting it asks first. - **Settings → Backup & Restore** exports settings, themes, extension preferences, projects, and layouts. Restore applies on the next launch and keeps a recovery copy in `Backups`. Existing projects are kept; matching projects receive the saved layouts. Server settings take effect after restarting the server. - Import supported 1.x settings and local projects from the installed app, a `.muxy` backup, or `settings.json`. Unsupported options are listed before import. A 1.x import adds to what is already there: existing projects, tabs, and workspaces are kept. A profile with no projects or workspaces yet imports the installed 1.x automatically, once, including its extensions. Profiles chosen with `MUXY_DIR` are left alone. Config files open in the system editor. Backups exclude live terminal sessions, paired-device credentials, extension packages, and project files. They keep the list of remote servers but not remote projects, which come back from their server. ## Updates ```mermaid flowchart TD UPDATE["Update available"] --> FITS{"Can the new version talk
to the running server?"} FITS -->|"yes"| NOW["Installs now · terminals keep running
server is replaced once no terminals are left"] FITS -->|"no"| CHOICE{"You choose"} CHOICE -->|"wait"| LATER["Installs once every terminal has ended"] CHOICE -->|"update now"| FORCE["Asks first · every terminal ends"] ``` When the new version can talk to the running server, checking **Also restart the server** in the update dialog replaces the server now too. Every terminal ends. ## Desktop features - **Composer.** Write a draft, with files or images, and send it to the active terminal or to every visible split. Each project keeps its own draft, and a failed send keeps it. - **Web views.** Extension pages as tabs, docked panels, popovers, or dialogs. They stay alive while hidden. Extension panels belong to a project: switching projects closes them, and switching back reopens them. - **Extensions.** Add tabs, panels, a sidebar, toolbar, rail, and status bar items, shortcuts, and background scripts. They are managed in Settings → Extensions, declare their permissions, and ask before sensitive actions. A coding agent can [build, change, and publish them](../extensions/agents.md). Most extensions made for Muxy 1.x work unchanged; see the [compatibility limits](../extensions/get-started.md#coming-from-1x). - **Git and AI.** For Git projects, the footer shows the branch and changes, commits and pushes with an AI-written message, and creates or manages pull requests. It uses an AI command-line tool you already have, chosen in Settings → AI. - **Open in IDE.** A titlebar button opens a project on this computer in the file manager or an installed editor. Picking an app from its menu opens the project there and makes it the button's default. - **Tips.** A tip appears from time to time as a toast in the window's bottom-right corner, and **Show Muxy Tip** in the command palette shows one on demand. Turn tips off from the toast or in Settings → Appearance. ## AI agents The server recognizes AI coding agents running in terminals and whether each one is working, waiting for you, or done. - Tabs, worktrees, and projects show the state of their agents, and "waiting for you" comes first. - The desktop app notifies you about agents in the background, and the server notifies paired phones. Looking at the terminal clears the alert in every app. - Detached terminals show no alerts, and no notification history is kept. ## Accessibility Screen readers and automation tools can find and operate Muxy's controls: projects, worktrees, tabs, panes, menus, forms and dialogs. Terminal contents aren't exposed yet.

# Product model The things Muxy is made of, and who owns them. ## The pieces ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph SERVER["Server · shared by every app"] PROJECT["Project"] WORKTREE["Worktree project"] SESSION["Terminal session"] PROJECT -->|"parent of"| WORKTREE PROJECT -->|"owns"| SESSION end subgraph APP["Each app · private"] WORKSPACE["Workspace"] TAB["Tab"] PANE["Pane"] TAB -->|"split into"| PANE end WORKSPACE -.->|"groups"| PROJECT TAB -.->|"belongs to"| PROJECT PANE -.->|"shows"| SESSION ``` | Piece | What it is | | --- | --- | | Server | Runs on a computer. Owns projects, terminal sessions, and server settings. | | Project | A folder on a server, with a name, color, and optional icon or logo. | | Home | The built-in project for your home folder. | | Worktree project | A Git worktree, shown under the project it came from. | | Workspace | A group of projects in one app, used to filter the sidebar. | | Tab | Belongs to one project and holds one or more panes. | | Pane | One view in a tab: a terminal, a web page, or an extension view. | | Session | A running terminal. Belongs to exactly one project. | | Paired device | A phone allowed to connect to the server. | **Shared or private.** Project names, icons, colors, and deletions reach every app, and so do the names renamed tabs give their terminals. Tabs, layouts, workspaces, and project order stay in the app that made them. ## Projects - A project is an identity that points to a folder. Two projects can point to the same folder. They share its files but are otherwise separate. - A new project is named after its folder. Its name, icon, logo, and color can be changed. - If the folder disappears, the project shows as failed and can only be deleted. An offline server does not make its projects fail. - Changing directory inside a terminal never moves it to another project. ## Home Every server has one Home project for the user's home folder. Quick Terminal and other one-off terminals live there. Home is always first in the sidebar. It can't be deleted, have worktrees, or join a workspace. A remote server's Home goes by the server's name. ## Workspaces A workspace is a named filter for the sidebar. A project can be in no workspace, one, or several, and a workspace can be empty. Deleting a workspace never touches its projects. Workspaces filter the projects of every server, under each server's heading in the sidebar. ## Worktrees A worktree project is a child of a normal project, pointing to a Git worktree's folder. You can create one from a branch or add a worktree that already exists. It takes the branch name and its parent's color, and has its own tabs. Worktrees can't have children of their own. Worktrees made outside Muxy show up automatically. A new project shows worktrees only if its repository already has some; turn them on or off from the project menu. After a worktree is deleted outside Muxy, its entry is removed automatically if it has no tabs in this app and no terminal history. ```mermaid flowchart LR PARENT["muxy
~/code/muxy"] --> FEATURE["feature-x
~/code/muxy-feature-x"] PARENT --> FIX["fix-login
~/code/muxy-fix-login"] ``` ## Deleting Deleting always asks first and explains what will end. | You delete | What happens | | --- | --- | | A project | It disappears from every app and its terminals end. Files stay on disk. | | A worktree project | The same, and its worktree folder is removed too. | | A project with worktrees | Its worktree projects are deleted too. Their folders stay on disk. | | Home | Not allowed. | ## Tabs and panes - A project can have any number of tabs, including none. - A tab splits into panes, side by side or stacked, as deep as you like. Closing its last pane closes the tab. - Drag a tab to an edge of the content to show it beside the others in a new group. Each group has its own tab strip. - Closing a group's last tab removes the group. - Tabs can have a custom title and color, and can be pinned. Pinned tabs stay first and can't be closed until unpinned. - A terminal's title is the one its program sets, otherwise the running program's name, otherwise its folder. Its pane header names the shell instead of the folder, and shows the folder beside the title. - The phone app titles terminals the same way, including the tabs it isn't showing, and a custom title names every terminal in the tab there too. - New terminals open in the project's folder, or optionally in the folder of the pane they were split from. - Terminals support selection, copy and paste, search, links, the mouse, input methods, and shell integration: jump between prompts and select a command's output. ## Project layouts Named layouts live in `.muxy/layouts/` inside a project or worktree. Use YAML, YML, or JSON files; the filename is the layout's name. Choose **Apply Layout…** from the project menu or the layout button in the top bar. Layouts are never applied automatically. Confirmation replaces that project's tabs in this app; terminals still shown by another app keep running. ```yaml layout: horizontal panes: - tab: name: editor command: nvim . - layout: vertical panes: - tab: npm run dev - tab: name: shell ``` `horizontal` means side by side; `vertical` means stacked. Splits can be nested. A leaf's `tab` is a command string or an object with optional `name` and `command`. Commands run in the project folder; a command list is joined with `&&`. Legacy `tabs` lists keep their extra entries as separate top-level tabs.

# Server model `muxy-server` runs the terminals for every app. It runs on its own, apart from the apps. ## Lifetime - An app starts the server if it isn't running. The server keeps running until it is stopped, or until an update replaces it once no terminals are left. - Stopping or restarting it ends every terminal but keeps settings and each terminal's saved content. Terminal programs are never restarted automatically. The desktop app keeps its tabs and starts a new shell in each pane once the server is back; the terminal UI closes the panes whose terminals ended. ## Sessions A session is one terminal. It belongs to the project it was created in; its current folder never changes that. A session keeps running until its program exits, someone ends it, or the server stops. Closing the last pane that shows it also ends it. Quitting an app, a crash, detaching, or the computer sleeping never ends it, and there is no timeout. ## Sharing a session ```mermaid flowchart LR DESKTOP["Desktop pane"] --- SESSION["Session"] TUI["Terminal UI pane"] --- SESSION PHONE["Phone"] --- SESSION ``` - Any number of apps can show a session and type into it at once. They share one size. - The first app to attach is the session's owner. When it leaves, the next one takes over. Ownership only labels the session in Existing Terminals; it grants nothing extra. - Panes you can't see, such as those in background tabs, still count as showing their session. They stop getting screen updates until shown again. ## Closing a pane ```mermaid flowchart TD CLOSE["Close a terminal pane"] --> DETACH{"Detach?"} DETACH -->|"yes"| KEEP["Keeps running
reopen from Existing Terminals"] DETACH -->|"no"| OTHER{"Another pane in any app
still shows it?"} OTHER -->|"yes"| KEEP2["Keeps running"] OTHER -->|"no"| END["Program ends and
its saved content is removed"] ``` - If a program other than the shell is running, you confirm once. Background jobs alone don't ask. - If the server is offline, the close waits and is decided on reconnect. - Ending a session or deleting its project affects every app, unlike closing one pane. ## History - Attaching shows the current screen and recent history. Older history loads as you scroll. - History size is a byte budget in server settings. The server reports how many rows it holds. - The server saves each terminal's screen and history, even when no app is watching, so it is still there after the program ends or the server restarts. A crash may lose the last moments of output. - Ended sessions and their saved output are automatically removed after 7 days. `muxy session list` shows live sessions; use `--all` to include saved ones. ## Git and files The server runs Git and file operations for its projects, such as worktrees, changes, and reading files. Every app, including phones, sees the same repository and files. ## AI activity - The server spots supported AI agents from the running program and what's on screen. It needs no plugins and works while no app is attached. Recognition is best effort. - It keeps at most one unread event per session, in memory only. Once seen, an event is cleared for every app. Restarting the server clears everything. ## Mobile access ```mermaid sequenceDiagram actor You participant Computer as Desktop app or muxy mobile participant Server as muxy-server participant Phone You->>Computer: Turn on mobile access and show a code Computer->>Server: Start pairing Server-->>Computer: One-time code, shown as a QR code Phone->>Server: Scan the code and pair Server-->>Phone: The phone's own credential Phone->>Server: Connect with the credential from now on ``` - Mobile access is off until you turn it on. - A pairing code works once, for five minutes, and only while it is on screen. - A paired phone can do what a terminal on the computer can, except manage mobile access, change server settings, stop the server, or run programs outside a terminal (`exec`). - Revoking a phone, or turning mobile access off, disconnects it at once. - A phone can pair with a server on another computer too, with `muxy --host mobile pair`. - The server sends paired phones push notifications about agents through the relay at `muxy.app`, encrypted so the relay can't read them. The server sends them, not the desktop app, so they work on headless computers too. They're on unless you pause them for every phone, which keeps the phones' registrations for 90 days so they resume when you turn them back on.

# Architecture The processes, the crates, and how data moves between them. ## Processes ```mermaid flowchart LR DESKTOP["Desktop app"] <-->|"Unix socket"| LOCAL TUI["muxy terminal UI"] <-->|"Unix socket"| LOCAL DESKTOP <-->|"SSH · muxy stdio
from another computer"| LOCAL DESKTOP <-->|"TLS · after pairing
from another computer"| NETWORK TUI <-->|"SSH · muxy stdio
from another computer"| LOCAL PHONE["Phone app"] <-->|"TLS · after pairing"| NETWORK PHONE <-->|"SSH · muxy stdio"| LOCAL subgraph SERVER["muxy-server · one per profile"] LOCAL["Local listener"] NETWORK["Network listener · opt-in"] CONNECTION["Client connections"] CATALOG["Projects"] S1["Session thread"] S2["Session thread"] LOCAL --> CONNECTION NETWORK --> CONNECTION CONNECTION <--> CATALOG CONNECTION <--> S1 CONNECTION <--> S2 end ``` - The desktop app ships the `muxy` and `muxy-server` executables, which are also released on their own. Either app starts the server if it isn't running. - The server keeps projects and which sessions belong to them. Apps keep tabs, panes, order, and workspaces. - The desktop app keeps a connection per server: this computer's, and one per other computer's server. A second connection to each carries extension work and remote file transfers, so they never wait behind terminal traffic. - Apps never include server code. They only speak the [protocol](./protocol.md). ## Crates ```mermaid flowchart TB APP["muxy-app"] --> UI["muxy-ui"] APP --> APPCORE["muxy-app-core"] APP --> CLIENT["muxy-client"] CLI["muxy-cli"] --> APPCORE CLI --> CLIENT MOBILE["muxy-mobile"] --> CLIENT CLIENT --> PROTOCOL["muxy-protocol"] APPCORE --> PROTOCOL SERVER["muxy-server"] --> TERMINAL["muxy-terminal"] SERVER --> PROTOCOL TERMINAL --> PROTOCOL ``` | Crate | Role | | --- | --- | | `muxy-app` | The desktop app. | | `muxy-ui` | Reusable GPUI components and native web views. No app state. | | `muxy-app-core` | The app model without UI, shared by desktop and terminal UI: layouts, workspaces, settings, extensions. | | `muxy-cli` | The `muxy` command: CLI and terminal UI. | | `muxy-client` | Connects to a server, starting a local one if needed. | | `muxy-mobile` | The client library for phones, with Swift and Kotlin bindings. | | `muxy-protocol` | Messages, encoding, screen types, and transports. | | `muxy-server` | The server: projects, sessions, history, Git, files, and mobile access. | | `muxy-terminal` | Wraps the Ghostty terminal and the PTY. | | `muxy-core` | Shared basics, such as folders, locks, the shortcut catalog, and the app language. | ## Typing a key ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant App participant Connection as Server connection participant Session as Session thread participant Shell App->>Connection: Input Connection->>Session: Forward right away Session->>Shell: Write to the PTY Shell-->>Session: Output Note over Session: Next tick, about 16 ms later Session-->>Connection: Rows that changed Connection-->>App: Screen frame App->>Connection: Ack, ready for the next frame ``` ## Inside a session ```mermaid flowchart LR PTY["PTY"] -->|"output"| READER["PTY reader thread"] READER --> OWNER["Session thread
owns the Ghostty terminal"] REQUESTS["Input · resize · attach"] --> OWNER OWNER -->|"input"| PTY OWNER -->|"changed rows"| OUTBOX["Outbox of each attached app"] OWNER -->|"checkpoints"| DISK["Saved screen and history"] ``` - One thread owns each terminal for its whole life. The Ghostty terminal isn't thread-safe, so everything else sends that thread messages. - A separate thread only reads the PTY and forwards bytes. Chatty programs produce many tiny reads. - Every tick, if anything changed, the session sends the changed rows and the cursor. If nothing changed, nothing is sent. - When output goes quiet after a burst, history is compressed. - A background writer saves the screen and history, so they survive the program and the server. ## Inside a connection ```mermaid flowchart LR READ["Reader"] -->|"input, acks, pings"| FAST["Handled right away"] READ -->|"everything else"| WORKER["Ordered background worker"] OUTBOX["Outbox
control messages first
one merged frame per session"] --> WRITE["Writer"] ``` - Each app has its own connection and outbox, so a slow app never slows a fast one. - The reader never waits on disk or on starting processes. - Screen updates merge: a newer frame folds into the one not yet sent, which goes out once the app acknowledges the previous one. - Replies and other control messages never wait behind screen data. ## Drawing in the app - For each visible terminal, the app keeps the screen rows as styled runs, plus any history it has fetched. - It repaints a pane only when a frame arrives or the view changes: one text line per row and one rectangle per color run. - Hidden terminal panes detach but keep their last screen and scroll position in memory, and the server still counts them as showing their session. They attach again when shown, displaying cached content first, even while offline. - The UI is built from `muxy-ui` components. Every app shortcut comes from one catalog, resolved through the keymap. Terminal preferences and key bindings live in `terminal.toml`, and the Quick Terminal's global shortcut is its own setting. ## Extensions and web views - Web views are native WebKit views and stay alive while hidden. They have no terminal or server state. - The app loads extensions, enforces their permissions, and asks before sensitive actions. Their scripts run in JavaScriptCore on their own threads. - File, Git, and process work goes through the server. Extension web requests run in the app and can't reach the local machine or private networks. - Marketplace packages are verified before they are installed. - Language packs are resource-only bundles. The app reads their catalogs, checks that each translation keeps its key's placeholders, and runs nothing from them. ## The browser - Browser panes embed [polybrowser](https://github.com/saeedvaziry/polybrowser), which wraps the system WebKit view and keeps profiles and history. - A page sits in the same native host as extension web views, so it hides under app content and shares the keyboard with Muxy's shortcuts. - The server knows nothing about browsers. `muxy browser` reaches the desktop app over its own socket in the profile folder, `app.sock`, which only this user can open. One JSON request gets one JSON reply. `muxy extension` uses the same socket, since extensions live in the desktop app too, and so does `muxy config`, to have the app reload the settings files it just changed. ## AI activity - Each session thread checks the running program, the title, and the screen against built-in rules to find agents and their state. - Apps get agent status from the server. They never read terminal output themselves. - One desktop app delivers system notifications, so alerts are never doubled. - The server sends paired phones encrypted push notifications through the `muxy.app` relay. See [Mobile](./mobile.md#push-notifications). ## Updates - If the new app speaks the running server's protocol version, the server keeps running and is replaced once no terminals are left. - Otherwise the update waits for every terminal to end, or ends them after the user confirms. - The old app bundle is kept until its server exits. - Linux user installs switch one symlink between complete version directories. Runtime leases keep old helpers available while apps, CLIs or servers use them; one previous version is also retained for rollback. Download checksums, package manifests and all three executable build identities are verified before activation. Package-manager paths are never replaced by this updater.

# Mobile Phones connect straight to `muxy-server` on the user's computer. The only service in between is the push relay at `muxy.app`, which forwards [push notifications](#push-notifications) it can't read. A phone connects in one of two ways: - **Paired, over TLS.** The phone reaches the computer on the same network, through a VPN such as Tailscale, or at an address added to the pairing code. - **Over SSH**, with the phone app's own SSH client. It runs `muxy stdio` on the computer, like `muxy --host` does, so no pairing or open port is needed. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph PHONE["Phone app · Swift or Kotlin"] VIEW["Screen and keyboard"] --> SDK["muxy-mobile
Rust client library"] end SDK <-->|"TLS 1.3 · pinned certificate"| SERVER["muxy-server"] SDK <-->|"SSH · muxy stdio
through the app's SSH client"| SERVER ``` ## Pairing ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant Computer as Desktop app or muxy mobile participant Server as muxy-server participant Phone Computer->>Server: Start pairing Server-->>Computer: Pairing link, shown as a QR code Note over Computer,Phone: The link holds the addresses, port,
certificate fingerprint, and a one-time secret Phone->>Server: Pair over TLS, trusting only that certificate Server-->>Phone: A token for this phone Note over Server: Keeps only a hash of the token Phone->>Server: Later: connect with the token ``` The computer lists its own addresses. One that phones reach by another name, such as a cloud server behind NAT, puts that name first with `muxy mobile pair --address`. ## Security - Mobile access is off until the user turns it on. - The phone trusts only the certificate named in the pairing code, so another machine can't pretend to be the computer. - Each phone has its own token and can be revoked at any time. Revoking closes its connection at once. - A connection that hasn't signed in gets nothing else from the server. - Paired phones can't manage mobile access, change server settings, stop the server, or run programs outside a terminal (`exec`). They can register only their own push token. - Over SSH, the phone logs in as the user and can do what that login can. Host keys and credentials stay in the app's SSH client. ## The SDK - `muxy-mobile` wraps the shared Rust client with UniFFI, which generates Swift and Kotlin bindings. Phones use the same protocol and flow control as the desktop app. - The SDK keeps each attached screen up to date. The app draws it and sends input. - Each release publishes the SDK for iOS and Android next to the desktop app. `scripts/build-mobile-sdk.sh` builds it locally. - A phone works with any server that shares its protocol version, so phone releases only need to follow breaking protocol changes. ## Push notifications ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant Phone participant Server as muxy-server participant Relay as muxy.app relay participant Platform as APNs or FCM Phone->>Server: RegisterPush, with its token Server->>Relay: Register the token Relay-->>Server: Registration id and secret Server-->>Phone: Status, and a key only the two of them hold Note over Server: An agent needs attention or finishes,
and 20 s pass with nobody looking Server->>Relay: Encrypted notification Relay->>Platform: Forward it Platform-->>Phone: Show it ``` - `muxy-server` sends them, with or without the desktop app. The relay holds the Apple and Google credentials, which can't ship in an open-source binary. - Each paired phone that turns notifications on gets its own registration and 32-byte key on each server. `remote.json` keeps the relay registration's id and secret, the key, and the phone's token. - The content is end-to-end encrypted with AES-256-GCM. The relay sees only the kind of event, and identifiers derived from the key that mean nothing to it. The phone shows decrypted text only when it authenticates under a key it holds. - An event is sent about 20 seconds after it happens, once per phone, unless it was acknowledged by then, the phone is connected, or push notifications or client access are off. - Tapping one opens the app on the event's terminal pane. - Only paired phones can register; phones over SSH have no device record. - The server reaches the relay over HTTPS with the web PKI's roots, through the proxy in `HTTPS_PROXY`, `ALL_PROXY`, or `HTTP_PROXY` unless `NO_PROXY` says otherwise. `MUXY_PUSH_RELAY` points it at another relay, such as one on this computer for testing. - `muxy mobile push off`, or the desktop's **Push notifications** setting, pauses them for every phone. The relay registrations are deleted at once, so nothing more goes to muxy.app. Each phone's token and key stay in `remote.json` for 90 days, and turning them back on registers those phones again with the same keys, without them reconnecting. - `muxy mobile push reset ` forgets one phone's registration and key without unpairing it; the phone gets a new key on its next connect. Revoking a phone, or the phone turning notifications off, does the same. The full contract between the server, the relay, and the apps is [push-notifications.md](https://github.com/muxy-app/muxy.app/blob/main/docs/push-notifications.md) in the `muxy.app` repository. ## Other computers A desktop app pairs with another computer the same way, from the pasted link, and reaches it like any remote server. It pairs as a computer, so the server gives it a desktop's rights: it may also run programs (`exec`), change server settings, and stop the server. Managing access stays with the computer itself. Its token is kept in `paired-servers.toml`, which only the user can read and backups leave out. Servers that predate this lack the `PAIRED_COMPUTERS` feature, and the app refuses to pair with them rather than pair as a phone. The full integration guide, with the API, setup, and error handling, is in [`crates/muxy-mobile/README.md`](../../crates/muxy-mobile/README.md).

# Protocol

How apps and the server talk. The exact messages live in `crates/muxy-protocol`.

## Connection

- The connection is a reliable byte stream: a Unix socket on the same computer,
  SSH to `muxy stdio` on another computer, or TLS for
  [paired phones and computers](./mobile.md).
- Traffic is split into channels. Channel 0 carries control messages, and each
  attached session gets its own channel for screen updates and input.
- Every frame starts with a small header: length, protocol version, channel, and
  message kind. Messages are CBOR with numbered fields. Screen rows use postcard.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant App
    participant Server
    App->>Server: Hello, with the versions I speak
    Server-->>App: Hello reply, with the chosen version and features
    App->>Server: Attach to a session
    Server-->>App: Screen and recent history, on a new channel
    loop While attached
        Server-->>App: Screen frame with changed rows
        App->>Server: Ack
    end
```

## Requests and replies

- Every request carries an ID and gets exactly one reply, in any order.
- A bad request, such as an unknown session or an invalid path, gets an error
  reply and the connection stays open.
- A request the server doesn't know gets an "unsupported" reply. That is how an
  older server answers a newer app.
- Malformed traffic closes the connection.
- For shared state, such as projects, sessions, and AI activity, the server
  sends a short "changed" notice and apps read the new state again.

## Screen updates

- A row is a list of style runs: text, its style, and its cell widths. Apps need
  no Unicode width tables.
- Frames carry only the visible rows that changed. A resize sends the whole
  screen.
- History is never pushed. Apps page through it and search it on request.
  A page, and the history an attach starts with, also list the images
  placed on those rows, as stills, with each placement's row counted from
  the first of them. Older servers list none.
- Image pixels go out once. The desktop app asks the server to stream
  images: a screen carries the pixels of an image's frame on show the first
  time it lists that frame, and later screens list it without them. The
  server decides as each screen goes out, so an app that falls behind gets
  only the newest images, as with rows. The app acknowledges a screen once
  the images it brought can be drawn, and keeps showing the old picture until
  then, so programs that replace images quickly, such as video players, never
  flash. A screen lists each image's frames by key, with the time each one
  shows. The app reads the other frames of an animation, and any it lost,
  on request, and plays animations itself. Moving an image or playing an
  animation sends no pixels.
- Apps that draw no images, and older desktop builds, ask the server to leave
  pixels out and read the frames they draw on request. An app that asks for
  neither, such as an older build still, gets the pixels of the frame on show
  with every screen that changes an image. Saved screens always carry their
  pixels.

## Flow control

Each attached session has at most one frame in flight to each app. While the
app is busy, newer output merges into a single waiting frame.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Server
    participant App as Slow app
    Server->>App: Frame 1
    Note over Server: Frames 2, 3, and 4 merge into one
    App-->>Server: Ack frame 1
    Server->>App: Frames 2 to 4, merged
```

Memory stays small, and a slow app jumps straight to the latest screen. Control
messages are always written first. Wire compression is planned but not built
yet.

## Versions

Two builds can talk when they share a protocol version, currently V2. Only a
breaking change bumps the version. Fields and enum values have permanent numbers
that are never reused, so a build skips fields it doesn't know and shows unknown
values neutrally.

| Change | Bumps the version? |
| --- | --- |
| Add an optional field or one with a default | No |
| Add an enum value | No |
| Add a request | No. Older servers reply "unsupported" |
| Add something the server must act on | No. Add it as a new request or feature, since older servers ignore unknown fields |
| Remove something | No. Stop using it and keep its number reserved |
| Change a type or meaning, make a field required, or change screen rows or the header | Yes |

Encoded samples of each version are kept in
`crates/muxy-protocol/tests/fixtures/v<N>` and are only ever added to. CI
checks that the current build reads every sample and that the last release
reads the current ones. Saved user data must never be lost when a format
changes.

## Requirements

| Part | Runs on |
| --- | --- |
| Desktop app | macOS 14 or newer, on Apple Silicon or Intel; experimental Linux packages target Ubuntu 24.04 on x86_64 and ARM64 |
| `muxy` CLI and server | macOS 14 or newer, or Linux with glibc 2.35 or newer, on x86_64 or ARM64. musl is unsupported. |

## macOS desktop app

Install with [Homebrew](https://brew.sh):

```bash
brew install --cask muxy-app/tap/muxy
```

Or download it yourself:

1. From the [latest release](https://github.com/muxy-app/muxy/releases/latest),
   download `Muxy-<version>-arm64.dmg` for Apple Silicon or
   `Muxy-<version>-x86_64.dmg` for Intel.
2. Drag **Muxy** to `/Applications` and open it.

To use [`muxy`](../features/muxy-cli.md) in your shell, choose **Install Command
Line Tool…** from the app menu. It links `~/.local/bin/muxy`.

The app updates itself, also when installed with Homebrew. Running terminals
keep going through most updates.

## Linux desktop app

Linux support is **experimental**, targeting Ubuntu 24.04 on x86_64 and ARM64,
with glibc 2.39 or newer and a working Vulkan driver. See the
[platform limits and WebKit sandbox setup](../tech/constraints.md#experimental-linux-desktop).

Choose the [quick installer](#quick-installer-with-in-app-updates) for in-app
updates, a [Debian package](#debian-package), or an [AppImage](#appimage).
All three include the desktop app, CLI and server. Use one format per channel
to avoid conflicting CLI commands.

### Quick installer with in-app updates

Install the Ubuntu dependencies once:

```sh
sudo apt update
sudo apt install curl python3 ca-certificates libfreetype6 libfontconfig1 libxcb1 \
  libxkbcommon0 libxkbcommon-x11-0 libwayland-client0 libvulkan1 mesa-vulkan-drivers \
  libwebkit2gtk-4.1-0 xdg-utils xdg-desktop-portal bubblewrap xdg-dbus-proxy
```

Install the **latest stable release** as your normal user, without `sudo`.
The installer detects your architecture and verifies the download:

```sh
curl -fsSL --proto '=https' --proto-redir '=https' \
  https://github.com/muxy-app/muxy/releases/latest/download/install-desktop-linux.py \
  | python3 - install
```

Open **Muxy** from Applications. The app, CLI and server install into
`~/.local/share/muxy-desktop` by default. Add `~/.local/bin` to your shell's
`PATH` to use `muxy <folder>` from a terminal.

### Debian package

Download `muxy-desktop_<version>_amd64.deb` or
`muxy-desktop_<version>_arm64.deb` from the
[latest stable release](https://github.com/muxy-app/muxy/releases/latest).
Use `dpkg --print-architecture` to check which you need. In your download
directory, replace the filename below with your download:

```sh
sudo apt install './muxy-desktop_<version>_amd64.deb'
```

APT installs the dependencies and adds **Muxy** to Applications, with `muxy`
and `muxy-server` in `/usr/bin`.

### AppImage

Install the [runtime libraries above](#quick-installer-with-in-app-updates), then
download `Muxy-<version>-linux-x86_64.AppImage` or
`Muxy-<version>-linux-arm64.AppImage` from the
[latest stable release](https://github.com/muxy-app/muxy/releases/latest).
Use `uname -m` to check: `aarch64` means ARM64. Replace the filename below with
your download and run it without `sudo`:

```sh
chmod +x './Muxy-<version>-linux-x86_64.AppImage'
'./Muxy-<version>-linux-x86_64.AppImage'
```

The first launch adds **Muxy** to Applications. AppImage uses **system WebKitGTK**.
If FUSE is unavailable, append `--appimage-extract-and-run` when launching it.

Muxy keeps an unpacked copy in
`${XDG_DATA_HOME:-$HOME/.local/share}/muxy-appimage/<bundle-id>` so terminals can
keep running after the window closes. This takes extra disk space. Use
`./Muxy-<version>-linux-x86_64.AppImage --cli <arguments>` for the bundled CLI,
or choose **Install Command Line Tool…** in the app to link it into `~/.local/bin`.

### Updates

- **Quick installer:** the app checks automatically; **Check for Updates** checks
  now. Stable installs stay on stable; beta installs stay on beta.
- **Debian package:** stop the server and quit Muxy, then download the newer `.deb`
  and install it with `sudo apt install`. There is no Muxy APT repository, so
  `apt upgrade` alone does not update Muxy.
- **AppImage:** quit the app, then download and run the newer file. Running
  terminals stay alive. If you linked the CLI, choose **Install Command Line Tool…**
  again from the new app.

Debian packages and AppImages do not use the in-app updater.

### Remove

Stop the local server in **Settings → Servers**, then quit Muxy. Stopping the
server ends its running terminals. Removal keeps your settings, projects and
saved session data.

- **Quick installer:** run the command below. For beta, replace `muxy-desktop`
  with `muxy-desktop-beta`.

  ```sh
  python3 "${XDG_DATA_HOME:-$HOME/.local/share}/muxy-desktop/current/install.py" uninstall
  ```

- **Debian package:** run `sudo apt remove muxy-desktop` (or `muxy-desktop-beta`).
- **AppImage:** delete the downloaded file, its matching unpacked copy listed
  above, and any CLI link or Applications entry pointing into that copy. The entry
  is in `${XDG_DATA_HOME:-$HOME/.local/share}/applications/com.muxy.app.desktop`
  (`com.muxy-beta.app.desktop` for beta). Do not delete a copy still used by
  another running app or server.

## Windows desktop app (beta)

Windows builds come with [beta](#beta) releases only for now.

1. From the [releases page](https://github.com/muxy-app/muxy/releases), open the
   newest `v<version>-beta.<N>` pre-release and download
   `muxy-<version>-windows-x86_64.zip`, or `-arm64.zip` for an ARM PC.
2. Unzip it anywhere and run `muxy-app.exe`. Windows warns about an unknown
   publisher, since builds aren't signed yet: choose **More info**, then **Run
   anyway**.
3. To use [`muxy`](../features/muxy-cli.md) in a terminal, add the folder to your
   `PATH`.

Terminals run PowerShell 7 when it's installed, and Windows PowerShell
otherwise. Not available on Windows yet: browser panes, the Quick Terminal,
remote servers over SSH, extensions that run scripts or show pages, and
automatic updates. Settings says why for each one.

To update, quit Muxy and run `muxy server stop`, which ends running terminals,
then unzip the newer beta over the same folder.

## CLI and server only

For a Linux computer or Mac without the desktop app. This installs `muxy` and
`muxy-server`.

### Homebrew

```bash
brew install muxy-app/tap/muxy-cli
```

Update with `brew upgrade muxy-cli`. On a computer you will reach as a
[remote server](../features/remote-servers.md), use the install script instead:
SSH sessions often don't have Homebrew on `PATH`.

### Install script

Set `VERSION` to the newest version on the
[releases page](https://github.com/muxy-app/muxy/releases/latest), without the
leading `v`:

```bash
VERSION=2.1.0
curl -fsSL "https://github.com/muxy-app/muxy/releases/download/v$VERSION/install-muxy.sh" \
  | sh -s -- --version "$VERSION"
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
```

The script picks the build for your OS and architecture, verifies its checksum,
and installs both commands into `~/.local/bin`. Add the `export` line to your
shell's startup file to keep them on `PATH`.

- **Update:** run it again with the new version and `--replace`.
- **Another folder:** add `--install-dir PATH`.

### Check it

Run `muxy --version` and `muxy-server --version`, then `muxy` to open the
[terminal UI](../features/terminal-ui.md). Updating them never restarts a
running [server](../features/server.md#lifetime); stop it to switch to the new
version.

## Upgrading from Muxy 1.x

Muxy 1.x offers Muxy 2 as an update, or you can install Muxy 2 over it. Unless
you already have projects or workspaces in Muxy 2, the first launch imports your
1.x setup: supported settings, shortcuts, local projects, workspaces, terminal
tabs, the default shell, and extensions. Projects, workspaces, and extensions
that could not be imported are listed, and your 1.x data stays where it was. To
import again later, open **Settings → Backup & Restore** and choose
**Import installed 1.x**; it adds to what you already have.

Some 1.x features work differently or are not in 2.x yet. Most extensions keep
working; see [Coming from 1.x](../extensions/get-started.md#coming-from-1x).

## Beta

The beta gets new features first. **Muxy Beta** installs alongside stable,
with separate settings and session data.

- **macOS:** download the newest `v<version>-beta.<N>` pre-release from the
  [releases page](https://github.com/muxy-app/muxy/releases). The app updates to
  each new beta.
- **Linux:** append `--channel beta` to the [quick-installer command](#quick-installer-with-in-app-updates)
  (`python3 - install --channel beta`), or download a beta `.deb` or AppImage
  from the releases page. Use the same [update method](#updates) as stable.
  The quick installer and Debian package provide `muxy-beta` and `muxy-server-beta`.
- **Windows:** see [Windows desktop app](#windows-desktop-app-beta).
- **CLI and server only:** give the [install script](#install-script) a beta
  version, such as `2.1.0-beta.1143`.

## First steps

The first launch opens a short welcome tour that sets up the essentials. Skip it
anytime, and replay it with **Welcome Tour** at the top of Settings. These are the
basics either way:

1. **Add a project.** Choose **Add Project** in the sidebar, or press `Cmd+O`,
   and pick a folder.
2. **Open a terminal.** `Cmd+T` opens a tab in the project. `Cmd+N` opens one
   in Home.
3. **Split it.** `Cmd+D` splits right, `Cmd+Shift+D` splits down.
4. **Quit freely.** Terminals keep running in the background. Reopen Muxy and
   everything is where you left it.

## Changing shortcuts

- In **Settings → Keyboard**, click a shortcut and press the new keys.
  **Reset** restores the default. Muxy refuses keys that are already taken.
- Changes are saved to `settings.toml` under `[keymap]`, for example
  `split_right = "cmd-alt-d"`.
- Terminal keys such as clear screen, line editing, and scrolling have built-in
  bindings. Add your own in **Settings → Terminal → Key bindings**; they take
  precedence while a terminal is focused.
- Commands from **Settings → Commands** and extensions can have shortcuts too.
- The Quick Terminal shortcut is set in **Settings → Quick Terminal**.

# Settings

Open the Settings tab with `Cmd+,`. Opening Settings again selects the existing
tab. Use the search box to find a setting. Changes apply immediately, and
Settings works while the server is offline. Close it with the tab’s close button
or `Cmd+W`; pending edits are saved.

On macOS, choose **About Muxy** (or **About Muxy Beta**) from the app menu to open
**Settings → About** in the same Settings tab.
